lessons.intro: You will learn how to read a rule written as if then, and to see exactly what it promises. This skill is the base of almost every reasoning question.

cards.b: An if then statement has two parts. The part after if is the condition, and the part after then is the result. It says that whenever the condition holds, the result must follow.
A rule like if it rains, the match is off says nothing about dry days. It promises nothing when the condition is false, so do not read it as a two way rule.
Look for words like if, whenever, every time, or provided that. Whatever follows those words is the condition, and the result is what the rule guarantees.

fig.title: Reading a rule
fig.note: The result follows only when the condition holds.

ex.q: Rule: If a number ends in 0, then it is divisible by 5. Which must be true?
o: Every number divisible by 5 ends in 0
A number ending in 3 is divisible by 3
A number ending in 0 is divisible by 5
Any number ending in 7 is prime
ex.why: The condition is ends in 0 and the result is divisible by 5, so every number ending in 0 must be divisible by 5. The rule says nothing about the reverse or about other endings.

lessons.tip: When a rule is not triggered, it tells you nothing about the result.

quiz.q: Rule: If a shop is open, it accepts cards. The shop is open. Can you conclude it accepts cards?
quiz.why: The condition is confirmed, so the rule guarantees that the shop accepts cards.

quiz.q: Rule: If you study, you will pass. Ana did not study. What does the rule say about Ana?
quiz.why: The rule only promises a pass when studying happens, so it says nothing when studying does not.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to link two if then rules so that one result feeds the next condition. Chaining lets you reach a conclusion that no single rule gives you.

cards.b: If the result of the first rule matches the condition of the second, you can join them. Write A to B and B to C as A to B to C, so A leads to C.
A chain only works if the result of one rule exactly matches the condition of the next. If the wording differs, you cannot safely connect them.
Drawing the chain as arrows helps you see each step. Each arrow is one if then rule, so you can read the full path from start to end.

fig.title: Following the chain
fig.note: Each step follows from the one before it.

ex.q: Rule 1: If a meeting starts at 9, then Sam arrives early. Rule 2: If Sam arrives early, then he gets a seat. The meeting starts at 9. What follows?
ex.why: Rule 1 says a 9 start means Sam arrives early, and Rule 2 says early arrival gives him a seat, so two steps link the start time to the seat.

lessons.tip: Chain only when the middle statement is worded exactly the same.

quiz.q: Rule 1: If a plant gets sun, it grows. Rule 2: If a plant grows, it needs water. A plant gets sun. What follows?
o: It grows, so it needs water
quiz.why: Sun leads to growth and growth leads to a need for water, so the chain gives that the plant needs water.

quiz.q: Rule 1: If a light is on, the switch is up. Rule 2: If the switch is up, the fan runs. The light is on. What follows?
quiz.why: The light being on confirms the switch is up, and the switch being up confirms the fan runs.

lessons.intro: You will learn the contrapositive, a way to rewrite an if then rule so that it is easier to test. It is one of the most reliable tools in logical reasoning.

cards.b: The contrapositive of if A then B is if not B then not A. It swaps the two parts and negates both of them. A rule and its contrapositive always say the same thing.
The converse, if B then A, is a different claim and can be false. Do not confuse the converse with the contrapositive, which is always logically equivalent to the original.
If a rule is hard to test directly, test its contrapositive instead. Finding one case where B fails but A holds would break the rule, so checking either form works.

fig.title: Rule versus its flip

pts: If rain falls, ground gets wet
If ground stays dry, no rain

fig.note: The two forms always agree, so either one works.

ex.q: Rule: If a number is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3. Which statement is the contrapositive?
o: If a number is a multiple of 3, it is a multiple of 6
If a number is not a multiple of 3, it is not a multiple of 6
If a number is not a multiple of 6, it is not a multiple of 3
If a number is a multiple of 3, it is not a multiple of 6
ex.why: The original is if P then Q, so the contrapositive is if not Q then not P, which here reads if not a multiple of 3 then not a multiple of 6.

lessons.tip: To write a contrapositive, swap the parts and negate both.

quiz.q: Rule: If a door is locked, then nobody can enter. Which is the contrapositive?
o: If nobody enters, the door is locked
If somebody can enter, the door is not locked
If the door is open, somebody enters
If the door is not locked, someone enters
quiz.why: Swapping and negating gives that if somebody can enter then the door is not locked.

quiz.q: Rule: If a bird is a penguin, then it cannot fly. Which statement is logically equivalent to this rule?
o: Birds that cannot fly are penguins
Birds that can fly are not penguins
Some birds that fly are penguins
quiz.why: The contrapositive of if penguin then cannot fly is if can fly then not penguin, which is equivalent to the original.

lessons.intro: You will learn to tell a condition that is required from one that is enough on its own. Mixing these two up is one of the most common reasoning errors.

cards.b: A sufficient condition guarantees the result. If A is sufficient for B, then whenever A happens, B happens, so having A is enough to get B.
A necessary condition must hold for the result to happen. If B needs A, then no A means no B, but A alone might not be enough.
Ask whether the result can happen without the condition. If it cannot, the condition is necessary, and if the condition alone guarantees the result, it is sufficient.

fig.title: Testing a condition
fig.note: Ask both questions about every condition you meet.

ex.q: To win a medal you must finish the race. Finishing the race is necessary for a medal. Is finishing the race sufficient for a medal?
o: No, finishing is required but not enough
It cannot be determined from this
ex.why: Necessary means you cannot get a medal without finishing, while sufficient would mean finishing guarantees one, and many finishers still win nothing.

lessons.tip: Necessary is a requirement, and sufficient is a guarantee.

quiz.q: Being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle. Which follows?
quiz.why: If something is a square it is guaranteed to be a rectangle, so every square is a rectangle.

quiz.q: Having a ticket is necessary to enter a concert. Does having a ticket guarantee entry?
o: Yes, a ticket always gets you in
No, you need a ticket but it may not be enough
quiz.why: A ticket is required, so it is necessary, but it may not guarantee entry, so it is not sufficient.

lessons.intro: You will learn the most direct valid pattern of reasoning, called modus ponens. Knowing exactly when it applies stops you from drawing unjustified conclusions.

cards.b: Modus ponens says: if A then B, and A is true, so B is true. Confirm the condition and you may confirm the result. The pattern is valid whenever both premises hold.
You can only use modus ponens when the condition itself is shown to be true. Assuming it, or guessing it, breaks the chain of reasoning.
Write the rule, write the confirmed fact, then write the result. Setting it out this way keeps you from mixing up which part is the condition.

fig.title: Rain and wet paths
fig.note: Every rainy day guarantees a wet path, and dry paths are not covered.

ex.q: Rule: If a runner finishes under 20 minutes, they get a certificate. Ben finishes in 18 minutes. What follows?
ex.why: Finishing in 18 minutes confirms the condition of under 20 minutes, so modus ponens gives the certificate.

lessons.tip: Only affirm the condition itself, never the result.

quiz.q: Rule: If a battery is charged, the phone turns on. The battery is charged. What follows?
quiz.why: The condition is confirmed, so the result follows by modus ponens.

quiz.q: Rule: If a shape has four equal sides and right angles, it is a square. Ruth's shape has four equal sides and right angles. What follows?
quiz.why: Both parts of the condition are confirmed, so modus ponens gives that the shape is a square.

lessons.intro: You will learn modus tollens, which lets you conclude that a condition is false when its result is missing. It is the logic behind many clever deductions.

cards.b: Modus tollens says: if A then B, and B is false, so A is false. If the promised result did not happen, the condition could not have held.
This pattern is valid, but only in this direction. Starting from A being false tells you nothing certain about B, so never draw that conclusion.
Modus tollens is useful in puzzles where you know the outcome. Each failed result rules out the conditions that would have produced it.

fig.title: Backwards reasoning
fig.note: Failing the result rules out the condition.

ex.q: Rule: If the alarm is set, the lights stay off. The lights are on. What must be true?
ex.why: The result, lights off, is false because the lights are on, so by modus tollens the condition, alarm set, must also be false.

lessons.tip: A missing result rules out the condition that would have caused it.

quiz.q: Rule: If a team wins the final, it gets a trophy. The team did not get a trophy. What follows?
o: It did not win the final
quiz.why: The result is false, so by modus tollens the condition must be false too.

quiz.q: Rule: If a room is empty, the lights are off. The lights are off. Which can you conclude?
o: Nothing can be concluded for certain
quiz.why: The result is true here, which does not confirm the condition, since the lights could be off in a room that is not empty.

lessons.intro: You will learn to chain three or more rules into one longer deduction. Longer chains are where careful, step by step work pays off.

cards.b: Long chains are just repeated modus ponens. Each rule feeds the next, so the first confirmed fact can travel all the way to a final conclusion.
Number the rules and write the new fact after each one. Losing track of an intermediate fact is the most common way a long chain goes wrong.
If one rule is missing or its wording changes, the chain breaks. Check that each result is exactly the condition needed for the step after it.

fig.title: A chain of facts
fig.note: Each stage must follow from the one before it.

ex.q: Rule 1: If a box is sealed, it is shipped. Rule 2: If it is shipped, it is tracked. Rule 3: If it is tracked, it is insured. The box is sealed. What follows?
ex.why: Sealed leads to shipped, shipped leads to tracked, and tracked leads to insured, so three steps of modus ponens give that it is insured.

lessons.tip: Write each intermediate fact down before moving on.

quiz.q: Rule 1: If a seed is watered, it sprouts. Rule 2: If it sprouts, it grows leaves. Rule 3: If it grows leaves, it makes food. The seed is watered. What follows?
quiz.why: Watering leads to sprouting, then leaves, then food, so three steps of modus ponens give that it makes food.

quiz.q: Rule 1: If a test is passed, the course is complete. Rule 2: If the course is complete, a certificate is issued. Rule 3: If a certificate is issued, the student gets a letter. Sam passed the test. Which is certain?
quiz.why: Passing completes the course, which issues a certificate, which brings a letter, so the letter is certain.

lessons.intro: You will learn to turn everyday rules, such as school policies and house rules, into clear if then statements. This lets you reason about what must happen in real life.

cards.b: Real rules often hide their structure. Rewrite a phrase like only if or unless as a plain if then statement before you reason with it.
A statement like you may enter only if you have a ticket means if you enter, then you have a ticket. It does not mean that having a ticket lets you in.
Many everyday rules have exceptions. Look for words like unless, except, or provided that, and treat them as extra conditions that can block the result.

fig.title: Two ways to read a rule

pts: If you enter, you hold a ticket

fig.note: Only if reverses which part is the condition.

ex.q: Rule: You may use the pool only if you have signed the waiver. Lee has signed the waiver. Can you conclude Lee may use the pool?
ex.why: Only if makes signing a requirement, but signing alone does not show that every other condition is met, so the conclusion is not guaranteed.

lessons.tip: Only if marks the requirement, not the guarantee.

quiz.q: Rule: Children may ride the bus only if an adult is present. Tom is a child riding the bus. What must be true?
quiz.why: Only if makes an adult a requirement, so a child riding the bus means an adult must be present.

quiz.q: Rule: Unless it is a holiday, the library opens at nine. It is not a holiday. What follows?
quiz.why: Unless means the rule applies whenever it is not a holiday, so the library opens at nine.

lessons.intro: You will learn how and and or change what a rule requires. Getting these two words right is essential before you solve harder logic puzzles.

cards.b: A rule with and requires both parts to hold. If the rule says A and B, then you need A and you need B, and missing either one breaks the requirement.
A rule with or is satisfied when at least one part holds. Both may be true, since or is usually inclusive unless the wording says either but not both.
The negation of A and B is not A or not B. The negation of A or B is not A and not B. Flip the connective and negate each part.

fig.title: Truth table for and
fig.note: Only when both parts hold does and come out true.

ex.q: Rule: A club member must be over 16 and have paid fees. Priya is 18 but has not paid. Can she join?
ex.why: The rule uses and, so both parts must hold, and although Priya meets the age requirement, unpaid fees break the other requirement.

lessons.tip: With and, one false part makes the whole rule false.

quiz.q: Rule: A scholarship needs a grade above 80 or an excellent essay. Jo has an excellent essay but a grade of 70. Does Jo qualify?
o: No, the grade is too low
quiz.why: Or needs at least one of the two parts, and the excellent essay satisfies the second part.

quiz.q: Negate this rule: 'Every entry needs a form and a fee.' Which is the correct negation?
o: Entries need a form or a fee
Every entry lacks a form and a fee
Entries need no form and no fee
Some entry lacks a form or a fee
quiz.why: The negation of and is or with each part negated, so some entry lacks a form or lacks a fee.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to remove wrong answers one clue at a time. Elimination turns a hard choice into a short list you can reason about.

cards.b: List every possible answer before you read the clues. This keeps you from forgetting a candidate and gives you a full starting set to shrink.
For each clue, remove any option that breaks it. Mark crossed options clearly so you never reconsider them by accident.
Keep going until a single option survives every clue. If more than one remains, you probably need another clue or a closer reading.

fig.title: Elimination routine
fig.note: Shrink the list one clue at a time.

ex.q: Four friends rank first to fourth. Ana is first. Ben is not last. Cy is second. Dee is not third. Who is fourth?
ex.why: Ana is first and Cy is second, and Ben cannot be last, so Ben is third and Dee is fourth.

lessons.tip: Write crossed options down so you never test them twice.

quiz.q: Four boxes, and one holds a prize. Box 1 is empty. Box 3 is empty. Box 4 does not hold the prize. Which box holds the prize?
quiz.why: Boxes 1, 3 and 4 are each ruled out, so only box 2 remains.

quiz.q: Four cards: Ace, King, Queen, Jack. The card is not Ace. It is not King. It is not Jack. Which is it?
quiz.why: Three cards are crossed out, so Queen is the only one left.

lessons.intro: You will learn to use a grid to track which items can go together, so that clues stay organised. A grid makes it hard to lose track in a puzzle.

cards.b: Put one list along the rows and the other along the columns. Each cell is a pairing you need to decide, such as which person owns which pet.
When a clue says two items match, mark that cell yes and clear the rest of its row and column. When a clue rules out a pair, mark that cell no.
Once a row has a yes, every other cell in that row must be no. The same is true for columns, and this often reveals the next forced pair.

fig.title: Ownership grid
fig.note: A yes clears its row and its column.

ex.q: Ana, Ben and Cy each own one pet: cat, dog or fish. Ben does not own a dog. Cy owns a fish. Ana does not own a cat. Who owns the cat?
ex.why: Cy has the fish, so Ana and Ben share cat and dog, and since Ana cannot have the cat, Ben has the cat.

lessons.tip: Every yes in a grid forces its row and column to be no elsewhere.

quiz.q: Dan, Eve and Fay each drink tea, coffee or juice, one each. Eve drinks coffee. Fay does not drink tea. Who drinks tea?
quiz.why: Eve has coffee, so Dan and Fay share tea and juice, and Fay cannot have tea, so Dan has it.

quiz.q: A cupboard has three shelves: top, middle and bottom. Pens, paper and tape sit one per shelf. Pens are not on the top. Paper is on the bottom. Where is the tape?
quiz.why: Paper takes the bottom, pens cannot be on top so they are in the middle, and so the tape is on top.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to combine partial clues so that together they cut the options down further than either one alone. This skill powers most logic puzzles.

cards.b: A single clue often leaves several options open. A second clue may remove others, and the two together can leave exactly one possibility.
Compare clues that mention the same item. Where their results overlap, you can often rule out a whole group of possibilities at once.
When a clue leaves only one possible position for an item, treat that as fact. Use it straight away, because it may unlock another clue.

fig.title: Options left after clues
fig.note: Each clue removes some of the remaining options.

ex.q: Four seats are numbered 1 to 4. Kim is not in seat 1. Kim is not in seat 4. Kim is in an even-numbered seat. Which seat is Kim in?
ex.why: The even seats are 2 and 4, and seat 4 is ruled out, so Kim must be in seat 2.

lessons.tip: Combine clues before deciding anything.

quiz.q: Five seats in a row are numbered 1 to 5. Lee is not at either end. Lee is in an odd-numbered seat. Sam is in seat 5. Where is Lee?
quiz.why: Not being at an end rules out seats 1 and 5, and the only odd seat left is seat 3.

quiz.q: Three cards are red, blue and green. Card A is not red and not blue. Card B is not blue. Card C is not green. Which colour is card C?
quiz.why: Card A must be green, so B and C share red and blue, and since B cannot be blue, B is red and C is blue.

lessons.intro: You will learn to solve puzzles where three people are placed in order, such as finishing places or seats in a row. You will use clues to build one clear order.

cards.b: Write the positions in order, first to last, as blank spots. Then place each clue into the spot it describes, starting with the most specific clue.
A direct clue fixes a person to a spot. A relative clue, such as A is directly before B, links two people so they must sit next to each other.
Once the order is filled, read every clue again and check it against the arrangement. This catches the common mistake of misreading one relative clue.

fig.title: Finishing order
fig.note: Fill the spots in order, then recheck every clue.

ex.q: Ana, Ben and Cy finish a race, first to third. Ben finishes directly after Cy. Cy is not first. Ana is first. What is Ben's place?
ex.why: Ana is first, so Cy must be second, and Ben finishes directly after Cy, so Ben is third.

lessons.tip: Start with the clue that fixes a single spot.

quiz.q: Three friends sit in a row: Ivy, Jo and Kai. Jo sits in the middle. Ivy sits at one end. Where is Kai?
quiz.why: Jo fills the middle and Ivy takes one end, so Kai must take the remaining end.

quiz.q: Three books, Red, Blue and Green, sit on a shelf in some order. Red is on the left. Blue is not on the right. Which book is in the middle?
quiz.why: Red takes the left spot, so Blue cannot take the right, which leaves Blue in the middle and Green on the right.

lessons.t: Mutually Exclusive Options and Ruling Out
lessons.intro: You will learn what it means for options to exclude each other, so that one being true makes the others false. This lets one clue settle several questions at once.

cards.b: Two options are mutually exclusive when they cannot both be true together. For example, a number cannot be both even and odd, so learning one rules out the other.
When a set of options is exclusive and exhaustive, one true option forces every other option to be false. Use this to remove many candidates in one step.
Not every pair of options excludes the other. A person can be both a teacher and a runner, so check whether the wording truly forbids both.

fig.title: Exclusive or overlapping
fig.note: Only exclusive pairs let one clue settle both.

ex.q: Each of five jars holds exactly one type of sweet: mint, lemon or cherry. Jar 2 is not mint. Jar 2 is not cherry. What type is in jar 2?
ex.why: Jar 2 is neither mint nor cherry, and because each jar holds exactly one type, the only type left is lemon.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the two options can ever be true together.

quiz.q: A card is either red or blue, and never both. The card is not red. What colour is it?
quiz.why: Red and blue exclude each other, so a card that is not red must be blue.

quiz.q: A coin is heads or tails, never both and never neither. The coin is not heads. What can you say?
quiz.why: Heads and tails cover every outcome and exclude each other, so not heads means tails.

lessons.intro: You will learn to count the possible cases that fit a set of conditions. Counting shows you which answer is most likely or which one must be true.

cards.b: Write out the cases that meet the first condition, then remove those that fail the next. A short list is far easier to check than a mental count.
If you pick one of 3 shirts and one of 2 pairs of trousers, there are 3 times 2, which equals 6 outfits. Multiply when the choices do not affect each other.
If a condition allows only one case, that case must be true. Counting can also show that a claim covers every possible case, so it must hold.

fig.title: Outfits from three shirts
fig.note: Each shirt pairs with two pairs of trousers, giving six outfits.

ex.q: A code uses one letter from A, B or C, followed by one digit from 1 or 2. How many different codes are possible?
ex.why: The letter and digit choices are independent, so you multiply 3 by 2 to get 6 codes.

lessons.tip: Multiply when choices are independent, and add when they are separate cases.

quiz.q: A class has 4 boys and 5 girls. How many ways can you pick one student to lead?
quiz.why: These are separate groups of one student each, so you add 4 and 5 to get 9.

quiz.q: A menu has 3 starters and 4 mains. How many starter and main pairs can you order?
quiz.why: Each starter pairs with each main, so 3 times 4 gives 12 pairs.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to use clues that say something is not the case. Negative clues are easy to misread, and one wrong reading can ruin an entire puzzle.

cards.b: A negative clue such as it is not the red one removes exactly one option. It does not say which of the remaining options is correct, so do not jump to a conclusion.
The statement not both A and B means that one of them is missing, not that both are missing. Keep these apart when you negate a clue.
Turn each negative clue into a list of what it still allows. Writing the allowed cases avoids mixing up what is excluded.

fig.title: Reading a negative clue
fig.note: Negatives remove options and do not pick one.

ex.q: Three runners are Ana, Ben and Cy. Ana is not first. Ben is not first. Who is first?
ex.why: The two negative clues remove Ana and Ben from first place, which leaves Cy as the only option.

lessons.tip: Each negative clue removes options, and it never selects one by itself.

quiz.q: A box holds a red, a blue or a green pen. The pen is not red. Which can you conclude for sure?
quiz.why: Not red leaves blue or green, so the safe conclusion is that it is one of those two.

quiz.q: A badge is not both gold and silver. Which is certain?
o: It is neither gold nor silver
It is at most one of the two
quiz.why: Not both means at least one is missing, so at most one of gold or silver applies.

lessons.intro: You will learn to check a candidate answer against every clue, not just the first few. A full check protects you from a tempting but wrong answer.

cards.b: Once you have a likely answer, read each clue and confirm it. A candidate that fits most clues but breaks one is still wrong.
Puzzles often include one clue that quietly eliminates the obvious choice. Give the strongest-looking candidate extra scrutiny, not less.
A correct answer satisfies all clues at the same time. If you find one violated clue, drop that candidate and move on to the next.

fig.title: Checking a candidate
fig.note: A candidate must pass every clue to win.

ex.q: Clues: The number is even. It is greater than 10. It is less than 20. It is a multiple of 4. It is not 12. Which number fits?
ex.why: Even, between 10 and 20, and a multiple of 4 leaves 12 and 16, and the clue that it is not 12 leaves 16, which passes every clue.

lessons.tip: A candidate that breaks one clue is not the answer, however close it looks.

quiz.q: Clues: It is a prime number. It is greater than 6. It is less than 9. Which number fits all the clues?
quiz.why: Only 7 is prime between 6 and 9, and 5 fails the greater than 6 clue.

quiz.q: A word has five letters, starts with a vowel and ends with the letter e. Which word fits?
quiz.why: Adore has five letters, starts with a vowel and ends with e, while each of the others breaks at least one clue.

lessons.t: Combining Clues in a Harder Puzzle
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine several kinds of clue in one puzzle, including direct, negative and relative clues. Harder puzzles reward careful, ordered work.

cards.b: Place the clues that name an exact spot first. Each fixed placement shrinks the work for the remaining clues and often unlocks the next one.
Negative and relative clues fit around fixed ones. Use the fixed positions to test each relative clue, since it often has only one valid arrangement.
Fill every position and read the whole list of clues once more. Harder puzzles hide small errors that only appear when every clue is checked together.

fig.title: Solved clue grid
fig.note: Each yes fixes one person's colour and clears the rest.

ex.q: Four people each have a different pet: dog, cat, fish or bird. Ann has no fish. The cat is not Ben's. Cy has the bird. Dee has the dog. Who has the fish?
ex.why: Cy has the bird and Dee the dog, leaving cat and fish, and since Ann has no fish, Ann has the cat and Ben has the fish.

lessons.tip: Solve the fixed clues first, then the ones that depend on them.

quiz.q: Three people, Ann, Bo and Cy, each drink one thing: tea, milk or juice. Ann drinks milk. Bo does not drink tea. Who drinks tea?
quiz.why: Ann has milk and Bo cannot have tea, so Bo has juice and Cy must have tea.

quiz.q: Four books are stacked top to bottom: A, B, C and D. Book A is above B. Book D is at the bottom. Book C is directly above D. Which book is at the top?
quiz.why: D is at the bottom and C sits directly above it, so A and B fill the top two spots, and A is above B, so A is on top.

lessons.intro: You will learn to pick out the conclusion of an argument and the reasons given for it. Once you can see the structure, weak spots are much easier to find.

cards.b: The conclusion is the statement the arguer wants you to accept. It is often signalled by words such as therefore, so, it follows that, or which means.
Premises are the statements offered as support. Words like because, since, and given that often introduce them, and they should justify the conclusion.
Some sentences are only background or examples. Ask whether a statement is supporting another, since only that supporting structure makes an argument.

fig.title: Premises versus conclusion
fig.note: Find the claim first, then its reasons.

ex.q: Every table is taken, so the cafe is popular. Which statement is the conclusion?
ex.why: Every table is taken is the reason, and so introduces the claim the arguer wants accepted, that the cafe is popular.

lessons.tip: Ask what the speaker is trying to prove, and that is the conclusion.

quiz.q: Because the bridge is closed, the bus will take the long route. Which is the conclusion?
o: The bus will take the long route
quiz.why: Because introduces the reason, so the closed bridge is a premise and the bus route is the conclusion.

quiz.q: Tom trains daily. Tom has run marathons. Therefore Tom is fit. Which is the conclusion?
quiz.why: Therefore marks the final claim that Tom is fit, while the first two sentences are the reasons given for it.

lessons.intro: You will learn to spot the unstated assumption that an argument needs in order to work. Many arguments look strong only because a hidden link is never checked.

cards.b: An assumption is a claim the argument needs but never states. If you remove it, the reasons no longer reach the conclusion, so it acts as a hidden bridge.
Read the argument and ask what else would have to be true for the conclusion to follow. The answer is often the assumption, and it is worth testing.
Once you find the assumption, check whether it is reasonable. A weak argument often depends on an assumption that is false or only sometimes true.

fig.title: The hidden bridge
fig.note: The unstated step links the fact to the claim.

ex.q: A shop says: 'Our coffee is the best because it is the most expensive in town.' What is the unstated assumption?
ex.why: The argument needs the assumption that a higher price means better quality, and without it, being most expensive does not prove the coffee is best.

lessons.tip: If the conclusion needs an extra step, that step is the assumption.

quiz.q: Argument: 'The new road must be safe because it was built by experienced engineers.' Which assumption is needed?
o: Experienced engineers reliably build safe roads
quiz.why: The argument only works if experienced engineers reliably produce safe roads, which it takes for granted rather than showing.

quiz.q: Ann will get the job because she has the most years of experience. Which assumption is needed?
quiz.why: Ann's experience leads to the job only if the employer rewards experience, which the argument assumes.

lessons.t: Spotting the Affirming the Consequent Trap
lessons.intro: You will learn to recognise affirming the consequent, a common invalid pattern. It looks like modus ponens but draws a conclusion the premises do not support.

cards.b: Affirming the consequent takes if A then B, then B is true, so A is true. The result being true does not show that the condition held, since other causes may exist.
Valid modus ponens confirms the condition. Affirming the consequent confirms the result instead, and that move is the trap, so check which part is being confirmed.
To expose the error, find another way the result could happen. If the result can occur without the condition, the conclusion does not follow.

fig.title: Spot the invalid move
fig.note: Confirming the result does not confirm the condition.

ex.q: If it rains, the grass is wet. The grass is wet. So it rained. What is wrong?
o: Wet grass has other causes, such as sprinklers
ex.why: The argument affirms the result, wet grass, to conclude the condition, and sprinklers could wet the grass without any rain, so the conclusion does not follow.

lessons.tip: Wet grass can come from many causes, so it cannot prove rain.

quiz.q: If a fruit is a lemon, it is yellow. This fruit is yellow. So it is a lemon. Which is the error?
o: It says yellow is a fruit
It assumes all yellow fruit is lemons
quiz.why: Being yellow is the result, and other fruit can be yellow too, so the argument affirms the consequent.

quiz.q: If a student studies, the student passes. Ben passed. So Ben studied. Is this valid?
o: Yes, if Ben is a student
No, Ben did not take the test
quiz.why: Passing is the result, and confirming it does not confirm studying, since Ben may have passed in another way.

lessons.t: Spotting the Denying the Antecedent Trap
lessons.intro: You will learn to spot denying the antecedent, a second invalid pattern that people often mistake for a correct inference. Knowing both traps protects you in arguments and in puzzles.

cards.b: Denying the antecedent takes if A then B, then A is false, so B is false. The rule only promises B when A holds, so A failing says nothing certain about B.
This pattern is the mirror image of affirming the consequent. Both are invalid, but modus tollens, which denies the result, is valid, so watch the direction.
A quick check is to look for another way B could still happen. If B can occur without A, then denying A cannot rule out B.

fig.title: Valid versus invalid
fig.note: Both look alike, so check which part is denied.

ex.q: If a call is urgent, it is answered first. This call is not urgent. So it is not answered first. Is this valid?
ex.why: Denying the condition, not urgent, to conclude the result is false is invalid, since a non-urgent call may still be answered first for other reasons.

lessons.tip: Denying the condition never proves the result is false.

quiz.q: If a dog is a poodle, it has curly hair. Rex is not a poodle. So Rex does not have curly hair. Is this valid?
o: No, other dogs may have curly hair
quiz.why: Denying the condition, not a poodle, cannot rule out curly hair, since other dogs may have it.

quiz.q: If a store is open, the lights are on. The lights are off. So the store is closed. Is this valid?
o: Yes, because the store is closed
quiz.why: Lights off denies the result, which correctly rules out the store being open, so this follows the valid pattern.

lessons.intro: You will learn why two things moving together does not prove that one causes the other. This error appears in headlines, advertising and everyday arguments.

cards.b: Two things can rise and fall together without one causing the other. The link may be a coincidence, or a third factor may drive both.
Ask whether a third factor could explain both trends. Hot weather can raise both ice cream sales and sunburn cases, without either one causing the other.
Even a plausible cause needs evidence about direction. Ask whether the outcome could have come first, and whether the timing supports the claimed cause.

fig.title: Three rising trends
fig.note: A hot-weather factor can drive all three trends.

ex.q: A study finds that children who own more books get higher test scores. The writer says books raise scores. What is the best objection?
o: Families with more books may also read more at home
ex.why: A third factor, such as home reading habits or family income, could explain both the book count and the scores, so books alone do not show they cause higher marks.

lessons.tip: Always ask whether a third factor could explain both trends.

quiz.q: Cities with more ice cream shops have more crime. Which claim does this data alone not prove?
quiz.why: The data only shows the two rise together, and city size could drive both, so causation is not proven.

quiz.q: A town adds a new park, and crime falls the next year. The mayor says the park caused the fall. Which is a strong objection?
o: Crime may have fallen for other reasons, such as new policing
quiz.why: Another cause, such as new policing, could explain the fall, so the timing alone does not prove the park caused it.

lessons.intro: You will learn why conclusions drawn from a small or unrepresentative group can mislead. Understanding this helps you judge surveys, reviews and news reports.

cards.b: A few cases can look dramatic by chance alone. Five people's opinions may differ wildly from those of a whole population, so treat tiny groups as weak evidence.
Ask how the group was chosen. If only people who volunteered or who were easy to reach took part, the result may not represent everyone else.
Larger, fairly chosen groups give steadier results. Also look at how much results vary, since a big spread means one average can hide a lot.

fig.title: Answers from five people
fig.note: Five answers cannot describe a whole town.

ex.q: A cafe asks 4 friends who all love espresso, then claims 'Most people in town love espresso.' What is the main flaw?
o: The friends are not a fair group to represent the town
ex.why: Friends who share a taste are not representative, so their views say little about the whole town, and that unfair choice of group is the flaw.

lessons.tip: Ask who was asked, and how many, before you trust the result.

quiz.q: A review site shows a product with 3 reviews, all five stars. Which claim is best supported?
o: It is the best product ever
Three reviews are too few to judge reliably
quiz.why: Three reviews is a very small group, so the perfect score is not yet reliable evidence about the product.

quiz.q: A poll of 1,000 people chosen at random finds 52% support a plan. A rival says the poll is worthless. What is the best reply?
o: The poll is too large to be useful
Only polls of 10 people are fair
A random group of that size gives useful evidence, with some error
quiz.why: A random group of 1,000 gives a far more reliable picture than a handful of people, although results carry a margin of error, so the poll is not worthless.

lessons.intro: You will learn to spot the false dilemma, where an argument pretends that only two options exist. Seeing the hidden alternatives often shows the argument is weaker than it sounds.

cards.b: A false dilemma presents a choice as either this or that, with nothing in between. Real situations often have several options, and the argument hides them.
Ask whether there is a third option, a middle ground, or a way to do both. If one exists, the either or framing is false.
Some questions truly have two answers, so do not reject every either or claim. Test whether the options really are exclusive and exhaustive before you judge.

fig.title: Testing a choice
fig.note: Real choices often have more than two options.

ex.q: Either we cut the library's hours, or the town will go bankrupt. What is the flaw?
o: Other options, such as cheaper funding or cuts elsewhere, are ignored
ex.why: The argument presents only two options, but cheaper funding or cuts elsewhere are real alternatives that it ignores.

lessons.tip: If an argument names only two options, search for a third.

quiz.q: You either love this city or you should leave it. Which reply best exposes the false dilemma?
o: You can like parts of it and still want change
quiz.why: That reply offers a middle position, showing that liking the city and wanting to leave are not the only two choices.

quiz.q: Students must choose between sport and music, or they will fail their exams. What is the flaw?
o: Students can do both, and exams depend on many things
Sport and music cannot both be done
quiz.why: The argument hides options, since students can often do both, and exam results depend on many factors besides this one choice.

lessons.intro: You will learn to recognise circular reasoning, where the conclusion is simply restated as a premise. Circular arguments look convincing because they repeat themselves.

cards.b: A circular argument assumes what it sets out to prove. The reason given is just the conclusion in different words, so no new support is added.
Try rewriting the reason in your own words. If it says the same thing as the conclusion, the argument loops back on itself and proves nothing new.
A good reason should be checkable separately from the claim. If you cannot test the premise without already believing the conclusion, the logic is circular.

fig.title: The loop
fig.note: The reason returns to the claim it was meant to prove.

ex.q: 'This book is excellent because it is a truly excellent book.' What is the flaw?
o: It is circular, since the reason repeats the claim
ex.why: The reason is just the conclusion restated, so the argument assumes what it set out to prove and gives no new support.

lessons.tip: If the reason and the claim mean the same thing, the argument is circular.

quiz.q: 'The law is fair because it treats everyone justly.' Which is the problem?
o: The law is not written down
Fair and justly mean the same, so it is circular
quiz.why: Fair and treats everyone justly say the same thing, so the reason only repeats the claim.

quiz.q: 'We know the theory is true, because it predicts the result, and it predicts the result because it is true.' Which is the problem?
o: The theory is supported by a test
The reasons assume the theory is already true
quiz.why: The argument uses the theory to prove itself, so it is circular, and an independent test is needed.

lessons.intro: You will learn to grade the strength of evidence, so that you can tell a solid argument from one that only sounds convincing. Not all support is equally reliable.

cards.b: Evidence ranges from personal stories to controlled experiments and large studies. Stronger evidence comes from methods that rule out other explanations.
Good evidence must bear directly on the claim, and it must be gathered carefully. A vivid story about one case is weaker than broad, relevant data.
Strong judgement considers evidence against the claim as well as for it. A single supportive result is weaker than a body of consistent findings.

fig.title: Strength of evidence
fig.note: Higher bars show more reliable kinds of evidence.

ex.q: Which is the strongest evidence that a new medicine lowers blood pressure?
o: A friend says it helped them
A controlled trial with many patients and a comparison group
ex.why: A controlled trial with many patients and a comparison group rules out other explanations far better than personal stories or headlines do.

lessons.tip: Ask what the evidence would look like if the claim were false.

quiz.q: Which is the weakest support for the claim that a school's new reading scheme works?
o: Test scores before and after across many classes
Comparison with a similar school that did not use it
A controlled study across several schools
quiz.why: Enthusiasm reflects opinion rather than measured results, so it says little about whether the scheme changes outcomes.

quiz.q: A claim is backed by 20 studies, 18 of which agree and 2 of which disagree. How should you judge it?
o: Ignore it, because two studies disagree
Treat it as reasonably well supported, while noting the disagreement
Count only the two disagreeing studies
quiz.why: A large, mostly consistent body of evidence is strong support, though the disagreements mean the conclusion is not beyond doubt.

lessons.t: Auditing a Whole Argument End to End
lessons.intro: You will learn a full method for auditing an argument from start to finish, bringing together every skill in this course. A clear routine lets you judge almost any claim you meet.

cards.b: Identify the conclusion and each reason, then write them as a short list. A clear map makes the next checks faster and reveals any missing link.
For each step, ask whether it is valid, whether a hidden assumption is needed, and whether the evidence is strong enough. Mark the weakest link you find.
Summarise the argument's strength in one sentence, naming its main flaw if there is one. A fair verdict is specific, rather than a general feeling that it sounds wrong.

fig.title: Audit routine
fig.note: Work in this order every time you audit.

ex.q: Argument: 'Everyone at the gym is fit. Sam goes to the gym, so Sam is fit.' Which best describes it?
o: Valid, but the premise is doubtful
ex.why: The logic is valid, since all gym goers are fit and Sam goes to the gym, but the weak point is the premise, which is a doubtful sweeping generalisation.

lessons.tip: A valid argument can still be weak if its premises are doubtful.

quiz.q: Which step should you take first when auditing an argument?
quiz.why: You cannot judge the argument until you know what is claimed and what supports it, so mapping comes first.

quiz.q: An argument is valid and all of its premises are true. What is it?
quiz.why: An argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are true, so this one meets that definition.
